name: The Right to an Explanation
title: The Right to an Explanation
answer: The right to an explanation concerns whether a person affected by an automated decision can obtain a meaningful account of how that decision was made. It sits at the intersection of data protection, administrative law, and algorithmic accountability. In practice it covers both individual requests for reasons and broader duties to document model logic, inputs, and weighting. The right is not yet uniform across jurisdictions, and its scope often turns on whether a decision is solely automated and produces legal or similarly significant effects.

sections.body: The right to an explanation concerns whether a person affected by an automated decision can obtain a meaningful account of how that decision was made. It sits at the intersection of data protection, administrative law, and algorithmic accountability. In practice it covers both individual requests for reasons and broader duties to document model logic, inputs, and weighting. The right is not yet uniform across jurisdictions, and its scope often turns on whether a decision is solely automated and produces legal or similarly significant effects.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The right runs on the legal and technical infrastructure that makes model behavior auditable. That includes data protection frameworks such as the GDPR, sectoral rules for credit and employment, and emerging AI-specific statutes. On the technical side it depends on logging systems, model cards, impact assessments, and interpretability tools that can surface feature importance or counterfactual explanations. Courts and regulators also rely on discovery mechanisms and expert evidence to reconstruct how a system reached a result.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: How the work is done varies by legal tradition and technical context. Lawyers and compliance teams map the decision pipeline from training data through model output to human review, then test whether an explanation is intelligible to the affected person. Technical staff may use post hoc methods such as LIME or SHAP, or design inherently interpretable models where the law requires it. The legal method is often comparative, drawing on guidance from data protection authorities and early case law to define what counts as meaningful rather than merely technical.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on transparency, contestability, and the imbalance of power between system operators and affected individuals. A weak explanation can mask discrimination, deny effective remedy, or shift blame to an opaque model. Governance measures include mandatory documentation, human review points, audit trails, and penalties for failure to provide required information. The site's tracking of active AI lawsuits and compliance pages reflects how quickly these duties are being tested in court and in regulatory enforcement.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The right is moving from a narrow data protection concept toward a general principle of algorithmic due process. Future rules are likely to specify what an explanation must contain, when it must be given, and how it interacts with trade secret claims. Technical standards for auditability and interpretability will become more formal, and courts will develop tests for sufficiency. Over time the right may extend beyond individual decisions to systemic explanations for high risk systems in public services, employment, and finance.
